conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello Mr. ___, I'm Dr. ___. You've just come back from your radiofrequency ablation procedure. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, doctor. I’m a bit groggy, but okay. My side is sore, nothing too bad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. You had the RFA on two liver tumors—segment 8 and 5—and we also drained about 5 liters of fluid from your abdomen. The procedure went well, and you were stable throughout.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that much fluid? No wonder I’ve been feeling so bloated. Was the fluid normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mostly yes, though it was a little bloody at first, which is why we’re keeping you overnight for observation. It cleared up by the end, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I see. Is there any risk of bleeding or infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There’s always a small risk, but your vital signs are stable, and your blood counts from earlier are holding steady. We’ll check them again tonight and in the morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I just reviewed your labs. Your hemoglobin is 9.2, which is a bit low but hasn’t changed since the procedure. Platelets are also low at 84, but that’s typical for your condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that why I sometimes feel tired?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Partly, yes. Your cirrhosis affects your blood counts. But right now, everything is stable, so no transfusion is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed your sodium is a bit low—130. It’s mild, but we gave you some albumin to help with volume status, since low sodium can be related to fluid shifts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this level, and it’s common in cirrhosis. We’ll monitor it, and you should check it again with your primary doctor soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your repeat labs look stable—hemoglobin still 9.2, sodium still 130. You’re doing well. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. What about pain? I might need something for the soreness at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve prescribed oxycodone 5 mg every six hours as needed. Just take it when necessary, and don’t drive or take it if you feel confused.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And what’s next for the cancer?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need a follow-up CT scan in four weeks to check how the treated areas are healing. Your hepatology team will review the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my regular meds? Should I restart them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, all your home medications—like aspirin, spironolactone, furosemide, and glyburide—should be continued as before. We’ve listed them on your discharge sheet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad things went smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Just follow up with your primary care provider for blood work and keep your hepatology appointment. Call if you develop fever, severe pain, or confusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’ve signed your discharge orders. The nurse will go over your instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care. I’ll make sure to keep those follow-ups.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy for a few days, and we’ll see how the scan looks in a month.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before you go—any questions I haven’t answered?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’m all set. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Safe travels home. We’re here if you need us.
